intro: Six problems in the style of the matriculation exam bring together the skills of measuring, uncertainty and graphs. Decide yourself how the data should be presented and what is read from the graph, and justify the precision of the result. The last problem combines measuring with the ideal gas law.

tasks.title: Hand timing on sports day
tasks.source_note: Invented example data: the numbers are calculated from a model, and small random variation has been added to them, as in a measurement.
tasks.text:
On the school sports day there is a $100\,\text{m}$ race. The distance has been measured with a measuring wheel, and its uncertainty is estimated as $0.3\,\text{m}$. Three timekeepers stand at the finish. Each starts a stopwatch on seeing the starter's flag drop and stops it when the runner crosses the finish line. The watches show hundredths of a second.

| Runner | $t_1\ (\text{s})$ | $t_2\ (\text{s})$ | $t_3\ (\text{s})$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liisa | $13.52$ | $13.90$ | $13.71$ |
| Mira | $13.80$ | $14.12$ | $13.96$ |

parts.text: Calculate Liisa's average speed in the units $\text{m/s}$ and $\text{km/h}$. Justify the precision of the result with the spread of the watch readings.

criteria.detail: The time is taken as the mean of the three watches, $13.71\,\text{s}$, and $v = \tfrac{s}{t}$.
$v = 7.29\,\text{m/s}$; the conversion by substituting $1\,\text{km} = 1000\,\text{m}$ and $1\,\text{h} = 3600\,\text{s}$ gives $26.3\,\text{km/h}$.
Three significant figures, because the watch readings differ from each other by tenths of a second; the justification is written out.
For example: about $26\,\text{km/h}$ is a brisk sprinting speed for an upper secondary student, clearly below the roughly $36\,\text{km/h}$ of a top sprinter.

parts.text: Estimate the uncertainty of Liisa's average speed from the uncertainties of the time and the distance, and state the speed with its uncertainty.

criteria.detail: The uncertainty of the time as half the range, $\Delta t = 0.19\,\text{s}$, and of the distance $0.3\,\text{m}$; the largest and smallest possible speed (or the sum of the relative uncertainties, about $1.7\,\%$).
$\Delta v \approx 0.12\,\text{m/s}$.
$v = (7.29 \pm 0.12)\,\text{m/s}$: two figures in the uncertainty, because its first digit is $1$, and the speed to the same decimal place.

parts.text: Mira ran in the same heat. Can these measurements show that Liisa was faster? Justify.

criteria.detail: Mira's time is $(13.96 \pm 0.16)\,\text{s}$ and Liisa's $(13.71 \pm 0.19)\,\text{s}$.
These measurements cannot show a difference; the overlap does not, however, prove that the times are equal.

parts.text: Assess the systematic sources of error in hand timing. Can you conclude for certain from the information in the problem whether the measured time is longer or shorter than the true time? Justify your answer. Also explain why the mean of several timekeepers does not necessarily remove a systematic error.

criteria.detail: The reaction delays of starting and stopping are treated separately: the watch starts with a delay $\tau_\text{start}$ after the start signal, and stopping also has a delay $\tau_\text{stop}$, which can be shorter because the finish can be seen coming.

criteria.text: The measured time is $t_\text{meas} = t_\text{true} + \tau_\text{stop} - \tau_\text{start}$, so the direction of the error depends on the difference of the delays and cannot be concluded for certain from the information given. A physically justified estimate of the direction is also accepted when its assumption is stated.

criteria.detail: The average part of the delays is in the same direction for every timekeeper, so the systematic error remains in the mean; the effect of random error usually decreases when results are averaged.

tasks.title: Thickness and density of copy paper
tasks.source_note: Invented example data: the numbers are calculated from a model, and small random variation has been added to them, as in a measurement.
tasks.text:
The side of a pack of copy paper says: $500$ sheets, size A4, that is, $210\,\text{mm} \cdot 297\,\text{mm}$, grammage $80\,\text{g/m}^2$. Grammage means that a sheet of one square metre would weigh $80\,\text{g}$.

A student measures the height of the stack of paper in the pack with a ruler as $51\,\text{mm}$. The smallest scale division of the ruler is $1\,\text{mm}$. The edges of the stack are not quite even, and the stack is compressed a little when the ruler is pressed against it, so the student estimates the uncertainty of the height as $1\,\text{mm}$. Without the wrapping, the paper weighs $2.49\,\text{kg}$ on a kitchen scale.

parts.text: Calculate the thickness of one sheet in micrometres with its uncertainty.

criteria.detail: $d = \tfrac{h}{N}$ and $\Delta d = \tfrac{\Delta h}{N}$, where $N = 500$.
Conversion by substituting: $1\,\text{mm} = 1000\,\mu\text{m}$.
$d = 0.102\,\text{mm} = 102\,\mu\text{m}$ and $\Delta d = 2\,\mu\text{m}$.
$d = (102 \pm 2)\,\mu\text{m}$: the uncertainty with one figure and the result to the same precision.

parts.text: Use the weighing to check whether the grammage of the pack is correct.

criteria.detail: The grammage is the mass of the paper divided by the total area of all the sheets, $N \cdot ab$.
Lengths in metres by substituting: $210\,\text{mm} = 210 \cdot 0.001\,\text{m} = 0.210\,\text{m}$; mass in grams.
Total area $31.2\,\text{m}^2$ and grammage $79.8\,\text{g/m}^2$.
The difference from the label $80\,\text{g/m}^2$ is less than one percent, so the label is correct to the precision of the scale.

parts.text: Calculate the density of the paper and compare it with the density of water.

criteria.detail: The mass of a one-square-metre sheet is the grammage and its volume is $1\,\text{m}^2 \cdot d$, so $\rho = \tfrac{\sigma}{d}$ (or for the whole stack $\rho = \tfrac{M}{N a b d}$).
$\rho \approx 783\,\text{kg/m}^3$, about $0.78$ times the density of water.
The answer with two significant figures, $780\,\text{kg/m}^3$, because the height of the stack, $51\,\text{mm}$, is a two-figure number.

parts.text: The student's partner suggests measuring the thickness of one sheet directly with the same ruler. Evaluate the suggestion. Also explain why the uncertainty of the height of the stack is larger than half the smallest scale division of the ruler.

criteria.detail: For one sheet the ruler would show $0$ or $1\,\text{mm}$: the reading uncertainty $0.5\,\text{mm}$ is about five times the thickness.
Measured from the stack, a reading uncertainty of the same size is shared by $500$ sheets.
The compression of the stack and the uneven edges add to the uncertainty, so the scale division alone does not give the uncertainty of the measurement.

tasks.title: An unknown liquid
tasks.source_note: Invented example data: the numbers are calculated from a model, and small random variation has been added to them, as in a measurement.
tasks.text:
In the laboratory there is a bottle of clear liquid whose label has come off. The liquid is probably water, ethanol or cooking oil. A student pours the liquid into a $100\,\text{ml}$ measuring cylinder whose scale division is $2\,\text{ml}$, and weighs the cylinder and the liquid together after each addition. The student estimates the uncertainty of the volume reading as $1\,\text{ml}$, and the resolution of the balance is $0.1\,\text{g}$. The empty measuring cylinder was not weighed.

| $V\ (\text{ml})$ | $m\ (\text{g})$ |
|---|---|
| $20$ | $137.6$ |
| $30$ | $145.7$ |
| $40$ | $155.7$ |
| $50$ | $163.9$ |
| $60$ | $183.4$ |
| $70$ | $183.0$ |
| $80$ | $191.8$ |
| $90$ | $202.0$ |
| $100$ | $210.3$ |

In the notes, the row $60\,\text{ml}$ says: “reading written down afterwards from memory”.

Densities from a data book: water $1.00\,\text{g/cm}^3$, cooking oil $0.92\,\text{g/cm}^3$ and ethanol $0.79\,\text{g/cm}^3$.

parts.text: Present the measurement results as a graph from which the constant term of the line can also be determined.

criteria.detail: $V\ (\text{ml})$ on the horizontal axis and $m\ (\text{g})$ on the vertical axis, evenly spaced scales; the vertical axis may start, for example, at $100\,\text{g}$ when this is marked.
All nine points in the right places; the point of the row $60\,\text{ml}$ stands out from the others.

criteria.text: The horizontal axis reaches zero so that the line can be extended to the vertical axis, and the points fill most of the graph.

parts.text: Fit a model to the points. Decide how you deal with the row $60\,\text{ml}$, and justify your decision.

criteria.detail: One straight line among the points, not a broken line; the line is not forced through the origin, because the balance also weighs the measuring cylinder.

criteria.text: The point of the row $60\,\text{ml}$ is about $10\,\text{g}$ above the line, and the note gives a reason for it: the point is left out of the fit.

criteria.detail: The omission and its reason are recorded; a point is not removed just because it differs from the others.

parts.text: Determine the slope and the constant term of the line with their units. What does each tell?

criteria.detail: Two points of the line far apart, for example $(20\,\text{ml};\ 137.0\,\text{g})$ and $(100\,\text{ml};\ 210.5\,\text{g})$.
$k \approx 0.919\,\text{g/ml}$ and $b \approx 118.6\,\text{g}$.
The unit of the slope $\text{g/ml} = \text{g/cm}^3$ and of the constant term $\text{g}$.

criteria.text: The slope is the density of the liquid and the constant term the mass of the empty measuring cylinder.

parts.text: Estimate the uncertainty of the density and conclude what the liquid is.

criteria.detail: The steepest and the shallowest line through the uncertainty bars: about $0.932$ and $0.908\,\text{g/cm}^3$, so $\Delta\rho \approx 0.012\,\text{g/cm}^3$ (by eye $0.01$–$0.02\,\text{g/cm}^3$).
The density of cooking oil is in the interval, those of water and ethanol are not; the result fits cooking oil, but other liquids can have the same density.

parts.text: The student wants to use the result to estimate how much $1.50\,\text{l}$ of this liquid weighs. Calculate the mass and assess whether using the result this far outside the measured range is justified.

criteria.detail: $m = \rho V$ without the mass of the measuring cylinder: $0.919\,\text{g/cm}^3 \cdot 1500\,\text{cm}^3 \approx 1380\,\text{g}$.
$1.50\,\text{l} = 1500\,\text{cm}^3$ and the answer $1.38\,\text{kg}$.

Density is a property of the substance, so $m = \rho V$ also holds for a larger amount at the same temperature; extending the line of the measuring cylinder beyond $100\,\text{ml}$, by contrast, would not be possible.

tasks.title: Checking a kitchen scale
tasks.source_note: Invented example data: the numbers are calculated from a model, and small random variation has been added to them, as in a measurement.
tasks.text:
A student doubts the kitchen scale at home and checks it with the school's calibrated weights, whose masses are known precisely. When empty, the scale shows $0\,\text{g}$, and its display shows whole grams. Each weight is weighed three times.

| Weight $(\text{g})$ | Readings $(\text{g})$ |
|---|---|
| $100.0$ | $102$, $101$, $102$ |
| $200.0$ | $204$, $204$, $205$ |
| $500.0$ | $510$, $511$, $510$ |
| $1000.0$ | $1020$, $1021$, $1020$ |

parts.text: What types of error can be seen in the data? Justify with the numbers of the data.

criteria.detail: Systematic error: every reading is larger than the mass of the weight, and repetition does not change this.

criteria.text: The error grows with the mass, about $2\,\%$ for every weight ($2$, $4$, $10$ and $20\,\text{g}$), but the reading of the empty scale is right.

criteria.detail: The random variation of the repetitions is at most $1\,\text{g}$, which is the size of the display resolution.

criteria.text: There is no gross error: no reading differs clearly from the other readings of the same weight.

parts.text: A friend says: “The scale shows grams, so when it shows $765\,\text{g}$ for flour, there is $(765 \pm 0.5)\,\text{g}$ of flour.” Evaluate the claim and give a better estimate of the mass of the flour.

criteria.detail: The resolution is not the uncertainty: it says nothing about the systematic error or about the variation of the repetitions.
Corrected mass $765\,\text{g} : 1.02 \approx 750\,\text{g}$.
The uncertainty is a few grams, for example $\pm 2\,\text{g}$, because the repetitions vary by about $1\,\text{g}$ and the correction factor is known only approximately.
The claim is wrong: there is about $(750 \pm 2)\,\text{g}$ of flour, not $(765 \pm 0.5)\,\text{g}$.

parts.text: Describe what the graph looks like when the horizontal axis has the mass of the weight and the vertical axis the mean of the readings, and explain how the graph shows the kind of error. Why does repeating the weighings not correct the error?

criteria.detail: The points are on a straight line through the origin whose slope is about $1.02$ and not $1$.

criteria.text: A constant term of zero tells that the zero point is right; a slope different from $1$ tells of a relative error.

criteria.detail: Repetitions reduce the effect of random error in the mean, but a systematic error repeats in the same way every time.

criteria.text: The error is corrected by dividing the readings by the slope $1.02$ or by calibrating the scale.

tasks.title: Speed of a toy car from a video
tasks.source_note: Invented example data: the numbers are calculated from a model, and small random variation has been added to them, as in a measurement.
tasks.text:
A group filmed with a phone a toy car that moved in a straight line on a level floor. In the video analysis program the scale was set to a $1.00\,\text{m}$ section of a measuring tape taped to the floor, and the front of the car was marked in the frames every half second. The timing began when the car was already moving.

| $t\ (\text{s})$ | $x\ (\text{m})$ |
|---|---|
| $0.0$ | $0.35$ |
| $0.5$ | $0.61$ |
| $1.0$ | $0.83$ |
| $1.5$ | $1.32$ |
| $2.0$ | $1.30$ |
| $2.5$ | $1.57$ |
| $3.0$ | $1.78$ |

An extract from the group's report:

> We joined the points in the graph with a line. We removed the point $t = 1.5\,\text{s}$, because it did not fall on the same line as the others. We calculated the speed from the last two points: $(1.78\,\text{m} - 1.57\,\text{m}) : 0.5\,\text{s} = 0.42\,\text{m/s}$. Because the result felt small, we also fitted a line through the origin, whose slope was $0.6341\,\text{m/s}$. Conclusion: the speed of the toy car is $0.6341\,\text{m/s}$.

parts.text: Evaluate the method and the conclusion of the report. Name at least four shortcomings and say why each weakens the result.

criteria.detail: A broken line also follows the measurement errors and is not a model; one straight line is fitted to the points.
The speed was calculated from two adjacent measurement points, so the error of either point matters a lot.

criteria.text: The line was forced through the origin, although the car was at about $0.35\,\text{m}$ when the timing began; that is why the slope is too large.
The point was removed only because it differed from the others; the reason should have been checked from the video and recorded.

criteria.detail: The result has too many figures and no uncertainty, and the result was chosen by what felt suitable.

parts.text: Determine the speed of the toy car with its uncertainty from the data. Justify how you deal with the point $t = 1.5\,\text{s}$.

criteria.detail: $t\ (\text{s})$ on the horizontal axis and $x\ (\text{m})$ on the vertical axis, evenly spaced scales.
A line with a constant term; the point $1.5\,\text{s}$ is checked from the video, and if it was marked in the wrong place, it is left out and the reason is recorded.
The slope from two points of the line far apart: about $0.477\,\text{m/s}$; the constant term $0.36\,\text{m}$ is the position of the car at the moment $t = 0$.
The steepest and the shallowest line, for example with bars of $\pm 0.03\,\text{m}$: about $0.492$ and $0.464\,\text{m/s}$.

parts.text: The group wants to improve the measurement. Suggest two improvements, one of which concerns a possible systematic error, and justify them.

criteria.detail: Error in the scale: if the measuring tape is at a different distance from the camera than the car, or the camera looks at an angle, all the positions are wrong in the same proportion.

criteria.text: The systematic error can be checked by measuring a known length on the car's path from the video, and the camera is placed perpendicular to the motion.

criteria.detail: A longer distance, more closely marked points and repeated runs reduce the uncertainty of the slope.
Each improvement is justified by how it changes the result or its uncertainty.

tasks.title: Air in a syringe
tasks.source_note: Invented example data: the numbers are calculated from a model, and small random variation has been added to them, as in a measurement.
tasks.text:
A student investigates how the pressure of air depends on its volume. The student connects a $60\,\text{ml}$ syringe to a pressure sensor with a short tube and pushes the plunger in slowly. No air can leak, and the temperature of the laboratory is $22\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The volume is read from the scale of the syringe, so the small air space $V_0$ inside the tube and the sensor does not show in the reading.

| $V\ (\text{ml})$ | $p\ (\text{kPa})$ |
|---|---|
| $12$ | $189.1$ |
| $14$ | $164.5$ |
| $16$ | $146.6$ |
| $18$ | $131.9$ |
| $20$ | $119.2$ |
| $22$ | $109.6$ |
| $24$ | $101.2$ |
| $26$ | $93.5$ |
| $28$ | $87.6$ |
| $30$ | $81.8$ |

parts.text: The student claims that the pressure of the air is inversely proportional to the syringe reading $V$. Test the claim with the data.

criteria.detail: The product $pV$ is $2269\,\text{kPa} \cdot \text{ml}$ at the reading $12\,\text{ml}$ and $2454\,\text{kPa} \cdot \text{ml}$ at the reading $30\,\text{ml}$.

criteria.text: The product grows in the same direction on every row, by about $8\,\%$ in total, so the growth is systematic and not random variation.

criteria.detail: The claim does not hold for the syringe reading; the reason may be the air space of the tube, which the reading does not include.

parts.text: Present the data as a graph in which the relationship is linear, and fit a straight line to the points.

criteria.detail: For example $\tfrac{1}{p}\ (\tfrac{1}{\text{MPa}})$ on the horizontal axis and $V\ (\text{ml})$ on the vertical axis; the vertical axis extends to the negative side.
The reciprocal of the pressure is calculated correctly for every row.

criteria.text: The choice is justified: when the temperature and the amount of air stay the same, $p(V + V_0)$ is constant, so $V = \tfrac{C}{p} - V_0$.

criteria.detail: One straight line among the points.

criteria.text: The line has been extended to the vertical axis.

parts.text: Determine from the graph the air volume $V_0$ of the tube and the sensor and the amount of substance of the air.

criteria.detail: Constant term about $-1.8\,\text{ml}$ and slope about $2.61\,\text{MPa} \cdot \text{ml}$.
The slope is $C = p(V + V_0) = nRT$, so $n = \tfrac{C}{RT}$.
$1\,\text{MPa} \cdot \text{ml} = 10^{6}\,\text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3 = 1\,\text{J}$ and $T = 295.15\,\text{K}$.
$V_0 \approx 1.8\,\text{ml}$ and $n \approx 1.06 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}$.
For example: $26\,\text{ml}$ of air at normal pressure is about a thousandth of a mole, because a mole of gas takes up about $24\,\text{l}$.

parts.text: Assess what assumptions the result requires and how the result would change if they did not hold.

criteria.detail: The temperature stays the same: the plunger is pushed slowly. In a fast compression the work heats the air, so the pressure is momentarily larger and $pV$ does not stay constant.
No air leaks: a leak would reduce the amount of substance during the measurement, and the product $p(V + V_0)$ would decrease.
Without $V_0$ the product $pV$ seems to grow with the volume, and the amount of substance and the relationship between pressure and volume would be interpreted wrongly.
When $V_0$ is added, $p(V + V_0)$ is almost constant, about $2600\,\text{kPa} \cdot \text{ml}$, so the data agree with the model.
